title: Shared Foundations, Open Source and the Construction of Private Ecosystems

paras: How public research, common standards and open software can become the foundations of privately differentiated products and platforms.

blocks.h2: 1. What counts as a public foundation?
paras: A technology firm can build a private business using resources it does not exclusively own: public scientific knowledge, roads and rights-of-way, radio spectrum administered by the state, university research, standards published by voluntary bodies, and open-source implementations. These are not interchangeable forms of “government-provided resources.” Spectrum is licensed or otherwise authorized, roads and rights-of-way are governed by law, publicly funded research has varying licensing conditions, and open-source code is distributed under its particular copyright license.

Consider an online retailer. It may use the publicly interconnected Internet, a privately owned access provider, Linux servers, an open-source database, a commercial cloud platform, privately owned fulfillment centers, and public roads for deliveries. Its advantage may lie in logistics, product selection, customer experience, data operations and contracts rather than ownership of the underlying Internet protocol.

blocks.h2: 4. Why large companies contribute to open source
paras: Contributing upstream can reduce duplicated engineering, attract contributors, improve compatibility, distribute maintenance costs, influence technical direction and encourage adoption of a wider ecosystem. Firms may open-source an infrastructure layer while selling hosting, support, security, devices, analytics or enterprise features. Other firms may keep core intellectual property proprietary. Neither strategy is inherently universal or permanent.

Example — Kubernetes: Google originally developed Kubernetes and donated it to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. Multiple companies now contribute to its development and sell managed Kubernetes services. The shared orchestration project enables competition at the infrastructure and service layer, but cloud-specific identity, networking and storage features can still increase migration costs.

Example — Linux: device makers, cloud providers and enterprise vendors all use the kernel. Some sell subscriptions and support; others use Linux inside proprietary devices or commercial cloud services. The kernel's openness does not automatically make all associated firmware, applications or service APIs open.
References support the institutional background and technical definitions. Interpretive comparisons and illustrative models are identified as analysis rather than established causal findings.
